patient.chief_complaint: Progressive unsteadiness and clumsiness of the right limbs over 2 weeks with slurred speech
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kwame Asante is a 43-year-old right-handed Ghanaian man who presents with a 2-week history of progressive right-sided limb incoordination and slurred speech. He first noticed difficulty writing on the classroom blackboard approximately 14 days ago, when his right hand began missing its target and producing jerky, inaccurate movements. Over the following days he developed an unsteady walking pattern, describing a feeling that his legs were not working together and that he was veering to the right. He also noticed that his speech had become slurred and he was occasionally stumbling over words, which his students and wife had remarked upon. He denies diplopia, facial numbness or weakness, dysphagia, limb weakness, sensory loss, urinary or bowel symptoms, or headache. He has no fever, weight loss, night sweats, rash, oral ulcers, or joint pain. He reports that approximately 14 months ago he experienced a 6-week episode of numbness and a heavy, weak feeling in his left leg, which gradually resolved without specific treatment. At that time, a general practitioner examined him and attributed the symptoms to lumbar disc disease; no imaging was performed. He has otherwise been well. He emigrated from Ghana to the United Kingdom 8 years ago. He has no personal or family history of autoimmune disease. He denies any prior episodes of visual loss, diplopia, or neurological symptoms apart from the leg episode 14 months ago. His hypertension has been stable on amlodipine. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substances. Review of systems is notable only for mild, intermittent fatigue over the past 6 months that he attributed to workload stress.

results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria
results.authors: Thompson AJ, Banwell BL, Barkhof F, et al.
results.key_findings: Revised criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time when DIS is met. Both symptomatic and asymptomatic MRI lesions can be used. Infratentorial lesions (including cerebellar and brainstem) count toward DIS. Simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI demonstrate DIT.

results.title: Multiple sclerosis
results.authors: Reich DS, Lucchinetti CF, Calabresi PA
results.key_findings: Relapsing-remitting MS accounts for approximately 85% of cases at onset. First-line platform therapies include interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate, and oral agents (dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide). High-efficacy agents (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, cladribine) reduce relapse rates by 50-70% compared to placebo. JC virus serostatus is critical before initiating natalizumab.

output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria require dissemination in space (DIS) in at least 2 of 4 characteristic CNS regions (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and dissemination in time (DIT), demonstrated by simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands. For RRMS treatment, the choice between platform and high-efficacy disease-modifying agents depends on disease activity, MRI burden, JCV serostatus, comorbidities, and patient preference.

interactions: Concurrent use with amlodipine 5 mg: No pharmacokinetic interaction; no dose adjustment required
contraindications: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) risk — contraindicated in patients with confirmed active PML
Concurrent use with another immunosuppressant or immunomodulator (combination increases PML and infection risk)
warnings: JC virus antibody index must be checked before initiation and every 6 months; high index (>0.9) with prior immunosuppressant use substantially elevates PML risk
Risk stratification: JCV antibody negative patients have low PML risk (<1:10,000); risk increases with duration of treatment and JCV seropositivity
Natalizumab must be administered via a REMS program (TOUCH Prescribing Program in the US) due to PML risk
Increased risk of infections including opportunistic infections; hold during acute serious infections
Infusion-related reactions may occur; pre-medication not routinely required but observe for 1 hour post-infusion
Screen for hepatitis B before initiation
output.formulary_status: Formulary with REMS requirements; prior authorization required
alternatives: Ocrelizumab 300 mg IV x2 doses (day 1 and 15) then 600 mg IV every 6 months (high efficacy, B-cell depleting, no JCV monitoring required)
Dimethyl fumarate 240 mg twice daily (oral, moderate efficacy, monitor lymphocytes)
Glatiramer acetate 40 mg SC three times weekly (lower efficacy, favorable safety profile, no monitoring burden)
Cladribine 3.5 mg/kg cumulative over 2 years (oral, immune reconstitution therapy, JCV monitoring required)
Fingolimod 0.5 mg daily (oral, moderate-high efficacy, requires first-dose ECG monitoring and baseline ophthalmology)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualising demyelinating plaques; ordering CT delays diagnosis and adds radiation without clinical benefit.
No cardiac indication in a typical MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia risk) — not as part of MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or DMT decisions; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard pre-LP imaging: confirm absence of mass effect or herniation risk on brain MRI before lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Establish dissemination in space (DIS) using brain MRI in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) — at least 2 of 4 regions required
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by identifying simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same MRI, or by CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (per McDonald 2017)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and initiating DMT
Order CSF analysis with paired serum to confirm oligoclonal bands and IgG index; verify CSF ACE to help exclude neurosarcoidosis
Correctly interpret ANA titer 1:80 (speckled, anti-dsDNA negative, anti-Smith negative) as below diagnostic threshold for SLE — insufficient to invoke CNS lupus in the absence of systemic features
Treat the acute cerebellar relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3–5 days); plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe relapses
Check JC virus antibody serostatus and index before considering natalizumab; if JCV-positive or JCV monitoring burden is unacceptable, ocrelizumab is the preferred high-efficacy alternative
Initiate a disease-modifying therapy after relapse stabilization; JCV serostatus, disease activity burden, patient preference, and comorbidities inform the platform vs. high-efficacy choice
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose MS based on a single cerebellar lesion or a single clinical event without confirming DIS and DIT per McDonald 2017 criteria

Do not interpret ANA positivity at 1:80 with speckled pattern and negative anti-dsDNA/anti-Smith as diagnostic of SLE or CNS lupus — this titer is borderline and occurs in healthy individuals and in MS patients
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient with a high index (>0.9) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML, particularly given escalating PML risk after 2 years
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose cardiac monitoring (bradyarrhythmia risk); avoid in patients with pre-existing significant conduction disease
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance MS therapy — ineffective long-term and harmful
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiating B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)

Do not attribute cerebellar enhancement with open-ring pattern to high-grade glioma or metastasis without full clinical context — open-ring enhancement is a high-specificity MRI sign of active demyelination
key_reasoning_points: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: McDonald 2017 requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it
Cerebellar and brainstem lesions count as infratentorial lesions for DIS under McDonald 2017 — this case meets DIS with periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord involvement

Simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing (right cerebellar peduncle) and non-enhancing (left cerebellar peduncle, periventricular, juxtacortical) lesions on a single MRI satisfies DIT without requiring a follow-up scan

Open-ring (incomplete ring) gadolinium enhancement with the ring opening toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of active demyelination (sensitivity ~80%), distinguishing MS from neoplasm or abscess which typically show complete ring enhancement

ANA positivity at low titer (1:80 speckled) with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies does not meet ACR/EULAR SLE criteria and occurs in up to 20-30% of healthy individuals and commonly in MS patients — do not conflate with CNS lupus
CSF ACE within normal limits and absence of leptomeningeal enhancement effectively excludes neurosarcoidosis, which can produce infratentorial demyelination and mimic MS on MRI

Short-segment (<2 vertebral segments), peripherally located spinal cord lesion at C3-C4 is characteristic of MS; NMOSD characteristically shows longitudinally extensive (≥3 vertebral segments) central cord signal

Prior episode of left leg numbness/weakness 14 months prior (attributed to disc disease without imaging) represents a likely first relapse — its documentation supports the polyphasic, relapsing-remitting course

JCV antibody index must be monitored every 6 months in all natalizumab-treated patients; ocrelizumab is the preferred high-efficacy alternative when PML risk is unacceptable or JCV seroconversion occurs

red_herrings.data_point: ANA positive at titer 1:80, speckled pattern
red_herrings.intended_effect: May prompt the agent to pursue CNS lupus (neuropsychiatric SLE) as the primary diagnosis and order an extensive lupus panel, delaying the MS workup or incorrectly attributing demyelinating lesions to SLE vasculopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: ANA at 1:80 speckled with negative anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies, normal complement, absent systemic SLE features (malar rash, serositis, arthritis, nephritis, cytopenias), and MS-typical MRI morphology (Dawson fingers, juxtacortical, open-ring enhancement) are not consistent with CNS lupus; low-titer ANA is a non-specific finding seen in up to 20-30% of healthy individuals and is common in confirmed MS

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward cerebellar-onset RRMS in a middle-aged Black African man. DIS (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and DIT (simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing lesions) are both established on the initial brain MRI, with OCB-positive CSF confirming intrathecal inflammation. The main cognitive challenge is correctly handling the low-titer ANA red herring (1:80 speckled) without over-pursuing a CNS lupus diagnosis in the absence of systemic SLE features or high-specificity anti-SLE antibodies.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Classic RRMS with cerebellar onset: DIS met across 4 regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, cord), DIT met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, CSF OCB positive. One clinically grounded red herring (low-titer ANA).
